title: What Is a CP2000 Notice for Crypto and How Should You Respond?
description:
A CP2000 notice is sent when the IRS believes income was not reported correctly, often based on 1099 forms such as the new 1099-DA for digital assets.

In many cases, crypto investors did report their income, but errors in how it was reported can trigger these notices.

The CP2000 process is a high-volume, low-cost way for the IRS to review tax returns and request additional payment. You typically have 60 days to respond.

The key issue is not missing income, but incorrect reporting. Responding incorrectly, especially emotionally or without proper documentation, can keep the issue open or increase the amount owed.

A proper response requires clear, structured information presented in a format the IRS understands.

👨‍⚖️ Clinton Donnelly, Founder of CryptoTaxAudit and known as the Crypto Tax Fixer, explains how CP2000 notices work and how crypto investors should handle them.

💼 What you’ll learn:
• What a CP2000 notice is
• Why crypto investors are being flagged
• How 1099-DA reporting errors trigger notices
• Why most responses fail
• How to properly respond to the IRS

FAQ: CP2000 Notices for Crypto Investors
Q: What is a CP2000 notice from the IRS?
A: A CP2000 notice is a letter from the IRS stating they believe you underreported income, often based on information from a 1099 form.

Q: Why are crypto investors receiving CP2000 notices?
A: Many CP2000 notices are triggered by mismatches between 1099-DA reports and what was actually filed on a tax return, especially when transfers or cost basis are not properly reflected.

Q: Does a CP2000 notice mean I am being audited?
A: No. A CP2000 is not a formal audit. It is a notice proposing additional tax based on IRS calculations.

Q: How long do I have to respond to a CP2000 notice?
A: You generally have 60 days to respond to a CP2000 notice before the IRS moves forward with their proposed changes.

Q: Are CP2000 notices always correct?
A: No. CP2000 notices are often based on incomplete data and assumptions, especially with crypto transactions.

Q: What happens if I respond incorrectly?
A: Responding incorrectly can result in paying more tax than necessary or escalating the issue further with the IRS.
